title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Advances in Diagnosis and Management
abstract: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Recent advances in diagnostic techniques, including rapid microbial detection methods and point-of-care testing, have improved early identification of causative pathogens. Empiric antibiotic therapy remains the cornerstone of treatment, with guidelines recommending会根据本地耐药模式和患者特异性因素选择方案。The role of biomarkers such as procalcitonin and C-reactive protein in guiding antibiotic stewardship has been validated in multiple clinical trials. Severe CAP requiring ICU admission benefits from early goal-directed therapy and close monitoring for complications including respiratory failure, septic shock, and organ dysfunction.
key_findings: Rapid diagnostic methods reduce time to appropriate antibiotic therapy
Procalcitonin-guided treatment reduces antibiotic exposure without worsening outcomes
Severity scoring tools (CURB-65, PSI) aid in site-of-care decisions

clinical_dimensions.definition: Community-acquired pneumonia is an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma acquired outside of a hospital or long-term care setting, presenting with symptoms of acute lower respiratory tract infection.
clinical_dimensions.symptoms: Typical presentation includes productive cough, fever, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and tachypnea. Elderly patients may present with altered mental status or generalized weakness without prominent respiratory symptoms.
clinical_dimensions.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires clinical assessment (symptoms, vital signs, physical examination) combined with radiographic evidence of new infiltrate. Microbiology testing guides targeted therapy when positive.
clinical_dimensions.treatment: Outpatient treatment: beta-lactam plus macrolide or fluoroquinolone monotherapy. Inpatient: beta-lactam (ceftriaxone) plus macrolide or doxycycline. ICU: beta-lactam plus macrolide or fluoroquinolone.
clinical_dimensions.complications: Common complications include pleural effusion, empyema, lung abscess, bacteremia, septic shock, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
clinical_dimensions.prognosis: Most patients respond to appropriate therapy within 48-72 hours. Failure to improve suggests resistant organisms, inadequate coverage, or complications requiring intervention.
